questions.prompt: An API requires a strong ETag in If-Match before replacing a document. The supplied tag no longer matches the current representation. Which status normally reports this failure?

choices.text: 412 Precondition Failed
304 Not Modified.
206 Partial Content, because part of the document may still match.
416 Range Not Satisfiable, because the validator is no longer current.

questions.explanation: If-Match is a precondition for performing the method and uses strong comparison. A false precondition normally yields 412 rather than cache or range statuses.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sources.claim: If-Match uses strong comparison for lost-update protection and a failed precondition normally produces 412.

questions.prompt: A server supports byte ranges and honors `Range: bytes=0-99` on a sufficiently long representation. Which status identifies that partial response?

choices.text: 201 Created.
206 Partial Content
304 Not Modified, because a Range request is always conditional.
412 Precondition Failed, because a request selected only some bytes.

questions.explanation: An honored satisfiable byte-range request uses 206. Range is not itself a cache validator or a failed write precondition.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sources.claim: A satisfiable byte Range request may produce 206 with Content-Range; an unsatisfiable range may produce 416 with the current length.

questions.prompt: An HTTP response carries stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error directives. Which interpretations follow RFC 5861? Select all that apply.

choices.text: stale-while-revalidate requires every client request to block until validation completes.
stale-if-error authorizes stale responses only when origin validation succeeds.
stale-while-revalidate can permit a stale response while revalidation runs.
stale-if-error can allow stale content when an origin request encounters an error.
Either directive makes a response fresh for an unlimited period.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: avoiding that blocking is the purpose of its stale window. B is incorrect: it applies to error conditions, not successful validation. C is correct: that extension permits serving stale content without blocking on revalidation within its window. D is correct: the extension covers errors such as network failures and server errors. E is incorrect: the extensions bound allowed stale use and do not redefine unlimited freshness.

sources.title: stalecache
sources.claim: stale-while-revalidate allows bounded stale responses during background revalidation; stale-if-error permits bounded stale responses on defined errors.

questions.prompt: A client sends only a weak validator in If-Match for a resource replacement. Which comparison rule governs matching?

choices.text: Weak comparison.
Lexicographic comparison that accepts any numerically newer validator.
Strong comparison.
A timestamp comparison inferred from the characters inside the tag.

questions.explanation: If-Match uses strong entity-tag comparison, so a weak tag cannot satisfy it. ETags are opaque rather than ordered values or encoded timestamps.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sources.claim: If-Match uses strong comparison for lost-update protection and a failed precondition normally produces 412.

questions.prompt: A single-part 206 response contains bytes 0 through 99 of a 1,000-byte representation. What does Content-Range describe?

choices.text: bytes 100-1000/1000, because it records bytes the server omitted.
bytes 0-99/*, because a server must hide every known total length.

questions.explanation: Content-Range names the inclusive start and end and, when known, the complete representation length. The final byte position is not exclusive.

sources.title: RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics
sources.claim: A satisfiable byte Range request may produce 206 with Content-Range; an unsatisfiable range may produce 416 with the current length.

questions.prompt: A cache operator separates normal revalidation latency from origin outages. Which directive behaviors are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A stale-while-revalidate window is expressed as a number of seconds.
A stale-if-error window limits how old an error fallback may be.
Without traffic, a stale-while-revalidate window need not trigger proactive fetches.
An error fallback is allowed forever once stale-if-error appears once.
stale-while-revalidate removes the need for ordinary freshness calculations.

questions.explanation: A is correct: the delta-seconds bound stale serving after freshness expires. B is correct: its delta-seconds restrict permitted staleness. C is correct: the specification discusses revalidation prompted by requests during the window. D is incorrect: the specified time bound still applies. E is incorrect: the extension starts from a response becoming stale.

sources.title: stalecache
sources.claim: stale-while-revalidate allows bounded stale responses during background revalidation; stale-if-error permits bounded stale responses on defined errors.
